To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the emotional well-being of older adults, in comparison to that of younger adults, is characterized by a greater tendency to experience positive emotions, a lower tendency to experience negative emotions, and a more balanced emotional profile.

1) emotional well-being increases across adulthood, and 2) this increase is related to cognitive-emotional mechanisms that support everyday functioning, for example, the ability to perceive and regulate one’s own emotions.

(1) the cognitive and emotional systems are closely linked in adulthood, with positive age trends in both, (2) these links have implications for real-world behaviour, such as work functioning, and (3) these links may be moderated by individual and contextual factors, such as gender, personality, and life experience.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the interplay of cognitive and affective factors in everyday functioning, with an emphasis on work.
understanding the nature of emotional functioning across adulthood.
the question: How can we predict and enhance real-world behaviour across adulthood, especially in the work context?

there is no evidence that the emotional life of the middle-aged and older adults is worse than that of younger adults.

the emotional well-being of older adults can be predicted by cognitive processes, and these processes can be targeted to improve emotional well-being.

the study of cognition-emotion links across the life course is a promising approach to understanding emotional aging.
